Introduction
Climate-sensitive disasters, such as wildfires and heatwaves, are increasing in frequency, duration, severity, and geographic distribution. The number of heatwave days in the US has tripled since 1960, and severe wildfires are projected to increase by 30% globally by 2050 [1,2]. These exposures often co-occur, creating compounded hazards that synergistically and disproportionately harm the health of vulnerable populations [3]. Health impacts include short-term increases in both emergency department utilization and in hospitalizations, as well as longer-term sequelae such as worsened cardiopulmonary health, disruptions in care, and mental health challenges, all of which are made worse by repeated exposures [4–8].
California’s environmental landscape presents unprecedented challenges for public health, with rising temperatures and prolonged drought conditions creating conditions for increasingly frequent and severe extreme heat events and wildfires [9,10]. Wildfires have become the leading source of ambient fine particulate matter (PM2.5) across the state, with recent events resulting in billions of dollars in damages and exposing millions of residents to hazardous air quality [10,11]. The increasing frequency and long-tail effects of extreme heat and wildfire smoke are putting significant new strains on healthcare systems and workers, which must adapt to these circumstances in order to effectively provide care during and following these events. Most disaster planning focuses on single events and related patient “surges” [12–14], but climate-related events are increasingly common, often recur seasonally, and frequently overlap, challenging conventional paradigms of disaster management [15,16]. These events also compromise the safety and functionality of health facility infrastructure, as well as the psychological and physical capacity of the healthcare workforce that is often subject to the same strains as patients.
Despite growing recognition of extreme heat and wildfire smoke as public health threats, critical knowledge gaps persist regarding how these events affect health system infrastructure and operations, whether and how facility-level preparedness strategies are implemented, and what barriers frontline healthcare workers face in providing climate-informed care [17,18]. Importantly, there is limited qualitative research capturing the perspectives of healthcare providers during extreme heat and wildfire smoke events, and this data is crucial to addressing operational and training needs, resource allocation, practical workflows, and implementation efforts critical to successful response on the ground.
This study addresses these knowledge gaps by exploring what frontline healthcare workers can tell us about current state of clinical and operational preparedness of healthcare facilities in the San Francisco Bay Area for extreme heat and wildfire smoke events. Through in-depth interviews with frontline healthcare workers in these Bay Area facilities, we aim to characterize existing heat and smoke preparedness plans, understand provider knowledge and training needs, identify resource needs and implementation barriers, and document provider experiences providing care during these climate hazards. Capturing a rich and diverse range of perspectives provides essential insights into the practical, real-world challenges of implementing preparedness strategies at the facility level—information that is largely absent from the current literature but critical for developing effective, context-specific adaptation measures.
Methods
Ethics statement
This study was approved by the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) Institutional Review Board (IRB 22–38277), including approval of the use of verbal informed consent. Participants were given a study information sheet prior to the interview that described the purpose of the study and what participation would entail. If they expressed interest in participating, a Zoom video interview was scheduled. At the beginning of each interview, the interviewer reviewed information about the study and answered any participant questions. Participants then provided voluntary informed verbal consent, which was documented by the interviewer in the study records.
Study design and setting
From June 2023 to December 2024, we conducted a qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with healthcare providers in the San Francisco Bay Area. This region represents a critical setting for examining healthcare facility preparedness for climate-related events. The region has experienced multiple significant wildfires, including the 2017 North Bay fires and the 2018 Camp Fire, which exposed millions of residents to hazardous air quality and resulted in substantial increases in respiratory hospitalizations [19–21]. In terms of temperatures, the region’s historically temperate coastal climate has made its infrastructure and populations inadequately adapted to extreme heat. Notably, the region’s healthcare facilities serve diverse populations with varying vulnerabilities to heat and smoke exposures, including communities with limited resources for individual-level protective measures.
The Bay Area includes nine counties served by a diverse array of health systems, from quaternary academic medical centers to safety-net hospitals run by departments of public health and private community hospitals. All face recurrent and overlapping climate-related extreme weather events, including extreme heat exacerbated by limited cooling infrastructure, wildfire smoke from regional and distant fires that PM2.5 levels, and atmospheric rivers that produce extreme precipitation and flooding that disrupts infrastructure.
Participants and recruitment
Eligible participants were healthcare providers who interfaced with patients in clinical or nonclinical roles at facilities in the San Francisco Bay Area. Participants were classified as “internal” (UCSF providers across campus locations) or “external” (community-based providers from San Francisco Department of Public Health [SFDPH] community clinics and other nonprofit care settings in any of the nine Bay Area counties). We aimed to recruit approximately equal numbers of participants from hospital and community health settings; however, despite substantial outreach efforts, fewer community-based providers overall were enrolled.
We used purposive sampling to capture varied clinical experience, expertise, and institutional roles within the healthcare settings. We were particularly interested in recruiting participants who held leadership or administrative positions in addition to their clinical roles, given their potential insights into the development and deployment of facility emergency response plans, as well as participants involved in climate-specific planning efforts (e.g., clinic-based working groups).
The study team compiled an initial list of potential participants based on referrals from project stakeholders, including UCSF faculty and SFDPH partners. Prospective participants were then contacted via email using a standardized recruitment script. Snowball sampling supplemented purposive recruitment; prospective participants were encouraged to share the invitation with interested colleagues, and interviewees asked at the conclusion of each interview to suggest additional contacts. Participants received no compensation.
Data collection
A semi-structured interview guide was developed by a team of three investigators (MM, JMZ, SDW) based on the study aims, a review of the literature, and insights from internal and external stakeholders [22–24]. Questions addressed providers’ experiences delivering care during extreme heat and wildfire smoke events, whether their facility had an emergency plan for these event types, and what resources were available or would be helpful for mitigating impacts. Interviewees were also invited to share anecdotes about experiences with other types of weather events. Interviews also covered barriers and facilitators to implementation of recommended public health strategies for preventing adverse health effects from climate-related events [25].
One-on-one interviews were conducted in English remotely using Zoom video. One of three investigators (ABR, NS, MM) conducted each interview, and all were trained by investigators (SDW, JMZ) on conducting qualitative in-depth interviews, covering skills such as rapport building, probing for details, and reflecting clarity of participants’ ideas. None of the investigators were known by the participants prior to data collection. Interviews lasted between 11 and 43 minutes. Interviews were recorded and transcribed verbatim, and field notes were generated from each session. Data were de-identified following analysis and all participants were assigned unique identification numbers.
Analysis
We used an inductive-deductive thematic approach to analyze the transcribed interviews [26].. This hybrid approach is especially well-suited to exploring relatively novel topics where some theoretical grounding exists, but the specific context remains underexplored. In this case, we sought to systematically characterize existing extreme heat and wildfire smoke preparedness plans and identify anticipated resource needs within established disaster management frameworks, while also enabling inductive exploration of emergent themes from frontline healthcare workers’ perspectives and experiences that may not be captured by existing frameworks and may reveal unanticipated barriers, facilitators, and experiential insights.
An initial codebook was developed by (MM, JMZ, NS) under the guidance of (SDW), based on the study aims and questions explored in the interview guide. The codebook was pilot-tested by (MM, JMZ, NS), each of whom coded a subset of transcripts and then met to compare coding, discuss discrepancies, and refine code definitions.
The broader analytic team (JMZ, MJ, ABR, MM, SDW) iteratively revised the codebook by reviewing transcripts and adding new inductive codes to capture emergent themes not reflected in the original deductive framework. They met regularly to review emergent codes, discuss their application, and reach consensus on the final codebook.
All transcripts were coded using Dedoose software (Los Angeles, CA: SocioCultural Research Consultants, LLC www.dedoose.com). Each transcript was double coded by two investigators (JMZ, DZ), and code application was iteratively reviewed and discussed until consensus was achieved to maximize coding reliability. Discrepancies between coders were discussed and iteratively reviewed until consensus was reached. Coded excerpts were then aggregated by code, and patterns across codes were organized into themes and subthemes through team discussion and review. Selected participant quotations were chosen to illustrate key findings.
Results
Twenty-nine participants were enrolled in the study. Twenty-four (82.8%) were physicians, three (10.3%) were nurses, one (3.4%) was a paramedic, and one (3.4%) was a community health worker. The majority (19, 65.5%) were hospital-based providers, eight (27.6%) worked in community clinics, and two (6.9%) held joint positions. Among physicians, the most common specialties included internal medicine (N = 5), pediatrics (N = 5), emergency medicine (N = 4), and family medicine (N = 3).
Infrastructure as vulnerability
According to informants, historically temperate weather in the Bay Area has led to lack of air conditioning in most homes and public facilities, increasing the area’s vulnerability to the health effects of extreme heat and poor air quality. This inadequacy in community infrastructure was felt to increase both patient and staff vulnerability as well as to increase pressure on health systems at relatively lower temperatures. Providers described infrastructural vulnerability in terms of community infrastructure and lower heat thresholds, Inadequate facility Infrastructure causing exposure, impacts on equipment, power outages, and the benefits of updated infrastructure.
Community infrastructure and lower heat thresholds. Informants described differences in regional infrastructure that can shift the temperature at which health impacts begin to emerge, with lower temperatures leading to heat-related impacts in the Bay Area. As stated by one provider:
I’m originally from the East Coast where every summer, it would be mayhem when the temperatures would get above 90 or so…in the Bay Area, we have a much lower threshold, because…so much of the population does not have access to air conditioning at home. (Physician, Hospital)
Inadequate facility Infrastructure causing exposure: Infrastructural inadequacies within healthcare facilities themselves, both large- and small-scale, were frequently described to limit the facility’s response during heat and wildfire smoke events and facilitate exposures to heat and poor air quality in clinical settings. Even when air conditioning was available, heat and poor air quality could overwhelm current cooling and HVAC equipment. Multiple respondents described how these exposures negatively affect patient safety and patient experience and have impacts on provider and staff comfort while performing daily tasks both in clinical and non-clinical areas (Table 1).
Emergency rooms and hospital lobbies were particularly vulnerable to poor air quality due to frequent intrusions of outside air from in-and-out traffic, as described by one physician.
We run HVAC systems, but the doors open widely [and] frequently to let in ambulance traffic. And we definitely have a problem with poor quality air intruding into the emergency department forcing providers to wear N95s...It is difficult to keep the temperatures cool, in normal working temperature, when it’s very hot outdoors, and it’s particularly difficult in the emergency department where you can’t keep the doors closed, because of ambulance traffic and patients coming and going. (Physician, Hospital)
Participants noted that settings serving higher-risk patient populations with inadequate infrastructural support, such as skilled nursing facilities or carceral institutions, may be particularly impacted (Table 1). As one provider described,
I think there are times where it feels like the [skilled nursing] facility’s ability to handle extreme heat seems limited... I’m very worried that ...if we had extreme heat, I don’t think our air conditioning...is equipped enough to meet appropriate cooling needs…The majority of the patients are generally older adults. And so they are more predisposed to extreme heat events...they’re at the rehab because they’re recovering after the hospital, they’re not fully healthy and at home. So they’re a vulnerable group in terms of heat related illnesses. (Physician, Hospital and Community Clinic)
Impacts on equipment. Other impacts within facilities included forced closure of uncooled inpatient units and failure of laboratory equipment, which resulted in outsourcing of lab tests and subsequent care delays and costs. Impacts extended to faulty ice machines, impacting the ability to keep patients comfortable on uncooled hospital floors. Providers also described direct impacts on clinical care when equipment requiring stable temperatures was compromised (Table 1). As one provider described,
We can’t give any vaccines because opening the fridge would then decrease the temperature below which or above which we can keep vaccines safely.... if the fridge temperature were to increase, then we would have to dump the thousands, tens of thousands of dollars worth of vaccines. (Physician, Community Clinic)
Power outages. There were also concerns about inadequate preparation for power outages. Not all facilities had adequate back-up power strategies, though some reported active work to mitigate this at their facilities. Multiple providers noted how power outages during extreme weather events significantly impact the ability to provide care (Table 1). As one provider described,
During the excessive rains this year, which I think are likely linked to climate change we had a power outage. When the power goes out in the hospital, only electrical outlets that are colored red continue to function.. Unfortunately, what we learned was that our clinic and urgent care, which sees relatively high acuity patients, did not have any red plugs. And it definitely raised some concern that we weren’t ready for this kind of eventuality. (Physician, Hospital)
Benefits of updated infrastructure. While most interviewees cited specific infrastructural concerns, few felt that achieving the necessary improvements was within their control or that improvements were keeping up with the increasing frequency of these events. Conversely, those who worked in facilities with updated infrastructure consistently noted its positive impact.
Our facility underwent a huge renovation…it’s really become night and day because our ventilation underwent a huge renovation as well. So we have really excellent ventilation and air filtration, heating and cooling. So now I feel like we could be potentially a resource. And that was definitely not the case before we underwent renovation. (Physician, Community Clinic)
Healthcare staff impacts
Impacts on healthcare staff during heat and poor air quality events were multifaceted and included direct effects on staff as members of the community as well as secondary impacts on their ability to perform their health system roles. Staff impacts were often described in terms of conflicting personal and professional responsibilities, physical toll, logistical impacts, impacts on ability to provide effective care, conflict between patient care and staff safety, and emotional strain (Table 2).
Conflicting personal and professional responsibilities. A common theme involved conflicting responsibilities. For example, providers may be caregivers for affected elders and children or need to assume unplanned care during the workday due to school closures, adding a source of significant additional stress.
For me, on a personal level, during the wildfires, I had a newborn at home. So that definitely added stress in terms of I knew that we were in the East Bay, we were nowhere near like the fires into like danger zones. But the air quality concerned me because I was thinking of how can I get the best air quality for my newborn in my house. And so we set up filters and stuff, but I was at work. So... that’s kind of the stressor there. (Nurse, Hospital)
Some respondents also had the impression that this stress may be especially pertinent for lower-resourced clinic staff, who may face greater disparities in access to protective resources at home (Table 2).
Physical toll on staff. Staff also described the direct physical burden of working through extreme heat and poor air quality, including fatigue, irritability, and dehydration (Table 2). As one provider described,
[When] we have a day, 80 something degrees outside, the offices might be 85, 90 degrees or more inside. And so, I find myself and I think a lot of staff, we get tired, we get irritable, we get sweaty, you know, it’s just really uncomfortable. I think the level of stress in the clinic is just generally higher under those circumstances. (Physician, Hospital)
Logistical impacts on staff. Heat and poor air quality events also created logistical barriers that prevented staff from reaching work altogether, from evacuations and road closures to hazardous commuting conditions. When staff were unable to work at their usual sites, providers also described downstream effects on staffing levels and, in some cases, on patient access to care (Table 2).
Impacts on ability to provide effective care. Indoor workers reported being most affected when cooling or air filtration in their facility was inadequate, with significant impacts on their ability to work effectively during heat events. As one provider described,
I do manage a team that do...central lines…their workspace has no AC so…it could be 90 degrees...When they do procedures...they are fully gowned and draped and they get their cap, the masks on, the goggles on, and they basically bake themselves in that attire as well as with PPE. So it’s really difficult when they’re inserting [a] line or [the] position is important. You get sweat dripping down your eyes and you can barely [see] it and you need to hit that [vein]. So it’s definitely a true challenge with the heat. That impacts directly our staff and our patient care and family and satisfaction. (Physician, Hospital)
Conflict between patient care and staff safety. Staff safety and patient care were sometimes in direct conflict, especially, but not only for outdoor workers. Providers reported having to weigh the risks to their staff with the desire to maintain services for their patients, as well as concerns for increased violence towards staff members (Table 2). For example, street medicine teams work outdoors, but might be unsafe doing so during extreme heat or wildfire smoke days when patients most need support.
I think the biggest test...was during the COVID pandemic...there was a pandemic going on, but there was also one of the largest wildfires in California history...we still had to do COVID outreach testing, engaging patients. But when the air quality index was so poor how do we weigh the benefit of sending out a team when the AQI was like above 100 sometimes above 150 right? So, and weighing that with the need to deliver patient care, and then also realizing that our patients that are more vulnerable to extreme heat events and also wildfire smoke, for example, respiratory illnesses, even cardiac illnesses. (Physician, Community Clinic)
Emotional strain. Staff reported being deeply emotionally impacted by the experience of living and working through these climate events (Table 2). They described being distracted by worry about the situation, both in the immediate sense and in terms of its future implications. As one provider described,
The wildfire smoke...it’s orange outside, the air was so filled with smoke that it was hard to breathe, just walking around. That was a major kind of wake-up call, and also [had an] emotional impact to our staff. Because I mean, it was visible, it was so kind of intimidating. It was quite scary. (Paramedic, Hospital)
System overload
Subjects agreed that clinical facilities are critical parts of community disaster response, including the response to climate and extreme weather events and their health impacts. Increased patient volumes, particularly in emergency department and critical care settings, and frequent callouts by staff were reported as drivers of health system strain. Providers described these impacts in terms of increased patient volume and acuity, inconsistent recognition of impact, labor intensive response measures, systemic capacity impacts, ad hoc response and use of available resources, and downstream impact of closures on patient access. (Table 3).
Increased patient volume and acuity. Emergency department providers in particular felt strongly that heat and poor air quality led to significant increases in patient volumes and acuity that was often overwhelming.
We had an event... when there was a heatwave...in San Francisco. And although the ambient temperature was not much above 100 degrees, we had 18 codes in the space of about an hour or an hour and a half from heat stroke, heat exhaustion, people, you know, largely elderly patients, but coming in with seizures, and extreme body temperatures of up to 107 degrees. (Physician, Hospital)
Since the tertiary care university system serves a wide geographic area, patient volumes were also described as being affected by more remote weather events, including influxes of patients seeking relief from poor air quality in other regions (Table 3).
Inconsistent recognition of impacts. In contrast, inpatient clinicians did not consistently report direct impacts of these events on admissions. One interviewed surgeon did not recall any cancellations or delays during extreme heat or poor air quality events. Medical inpatient services generally did not attribute changes in patient census to heat or smoke, though such connections were sometimes recognized retrospectively. Underlying patterns in access to care and delayed clinical effects may shape whether changes in patient volume were attributed to heat and air quality events, as one provider described:
The wildfire smoke. It’s interesting. No, I didn’t see an uptick in asthma exacerbations at that time, during the most recent surge in 2020. However, that was at a time when shelter in place orders were standard. And patients were quite reluctant to come to care. And we were encountering a number of phone calls from patients asking for medication refills. And on further questioning, we realized that many of those children were actively having asthma exacerbations that ordinarily would have come to clinic. So I think that we severely underreported the respiratory impact of wildfire smoke during that wildfire season in 2020. (Physician, Hospital)
Labor intensive response measures. In addition to patient flow impacts on the larger health system, caring for patients during heat and wildfire smoke events adds additional tasks to staff’s daily responsibilities. Among affected staff, cognitive demand was increased, including finding workarounds for infrastructure failures and developing ad hoc means of supporting patient care activities (Table 3). Routine tasks often took longer or caused more discomfort during these events, as one nurse described:
I see that staff not only are trying to coordinate the care that a patient needs, but they’re also trying to address the discomfort that patients are in because it’s too hot, or they’re trying to also not only address it, but also help to mitigate it. So they spend some time cooling, getting equipment to help cool patients down, opening windows, trying to perhaps give baths to help cool patients down. (Nurse, Hospital)
Although fans, ice packs, and cooling blankets were available for inpatient services, infection control policies, intended to improve patient safety under normal circumstances, often posed barriers to implementing heat mitigation strategies such as fans.
For fans…it’s not super helpful, [it’s] warm air...but we’re not allowed to use fans in inpatient rooms, for infection control reasons. Because you circulate germs and bacteria and dust. Or if it’s a private room, you can use it, but you have to close the patient’s door and on a heated day, patients will not want you to close the door for that circulation. So you know we’re losing battles for the hot months in those units. (Nurse, Hospital)
Ad hoc response and use of available resources.
This lack of formal and integrated guidance and planning has led to significant improvisation and innovation with respect to both planning and response. For example, a carceral facility in the region now identifies high-risk patients in a registry ahead of time to minimize health impacts during these events.
During events, providers described providing patients with what resources they had on hand, including physical supplies such as masks or water, as well as information about cooling centers and health and air quality safety. When institutional resources were not available, especially in smaller outpatient clinics, many used their own resources to purchase extra fans, air filters, or air quality monitors.
We quite literally bought air purifiers. Like, my parents donated an air purifier because they had an extra one. We responded in the immediate sense, we were like, we’ve got to get this smoke out and be able to open a clinic. And so... [we] got on Amazon and ordered room air purifiers. (Physician, Hospital)
Several providers also noticed the efforts of facilities and engineering in setting up ad hoc mitigation strategies, like setting up air scrubbers at entrances, though opinions on effectiveness varied. Providers also described improvisational use of equipment for patient care, with one provider describing using body bags to bring in extra ice to lay out on gurneys to cool patients. Organized responses in some facilities and clinics involved similarly high-effort interventions, including individual checks on patients or converting visits to telehealth whenever possible to protect patients.
What we try to do is in the mornings, we try to call everyone in and say, hey, we’re gonna change it to telehealth don’t come in, it’s very dangerous outside. Especially when you have patients that are in chronic care management... you don’t want them to come in and expose themselves. So what we ended up doing, it’s full team effort, we get eligibility workers, health workers like myself, MA’s, we all get a list... let’s get all the morning patients called in. Whether that be, you know, 40 60, 80 patients that we’re calling in that morning, we call them and we let them know don’t come in. (Community Health Worker, Community Clinic)
Systemic capacity Impacts. Clinician concerns about patient safety and risk of readmission may delay discharge and drive prolonged lengths of stay, given a sense that more patients return to the hospital, or “bounce back,” during these events (Table 3). These concerns may prolong patient surge status, increase overcrowding, and further delay access to care. This hesitancy was clearest among clinicians caring for especially vulnerable patients, such as newborns, where discharge may be delayed if conditions in the community feel unsafe. One pediatrician described,
Having to make plans or adjust discharges for babies and their families because of how poor the outdoor air quality is, like asking if the family can leave between this hour and this hour, because it seems like that’s when the smoke is going to clear a little bit. (Physician, Hospital)
Many participants agreed that systems constantly operating at capacity limits flexibility and thus the ability to respond to these emergencies.
We do recognize that every one of these events impacts the emergency department directly, because [it’s] really the only place people have to go when any event occurs. Again, the medical system is at its breaking point, I would say or at least certainly at capacity. And so the idea that we have this added capacity to accommodate the increased visits that inevitably come with heat waves or air pollution issues, is I think naive, I think we have to accept that we are operating at maximum capacity. So when those happen, they do tend to overwhelm us. (Physician, Hospital)
Downstream impact of closures on patient access. There were also significant concerns raised about the downstream impact on patients of shutting down services in response to unsafe conditions.
I will say, though, that there was...the legendary orange day that we had in San Francisco where there was a lot of chatter in our leadership group about whether to even open clinic, reasoning that patients might think this is like the end of days, it was so bizarre. And there were a couple of days when the air quality index was so bad and so severe, that we considered closing for the safety, both of patients and of providers. But the reality of our practice is that closing is not an option. There are too many stakeholders that depend on us being open, especially for urgent care. (Physician, Hospital)
Similar dilemmas arose when facility conditions themselves became unsafe for continued operation, whether due to indoor heat or understaffing, forcing providers to weigh continued operation against safety for both patients and staff (Table 3).
Planning Gaps: Variability and operational uncertainty
Finally, providers described substantial variability in their awareness of, and confidence in, emergency plans for heat and poor air quality events, shaped by limited awareness of emergency plans, lack of guidance around best practices, and lack of prioritization and funding for climate emergencies. Community level response and preparation were also described. (Table 4).
Limited awareness of emergency plans. Most respondents endorsed knowing little to nothing about the specifics of emergency planning for their facility’s operations during heat and AQI events, including whether such plans exist, who develops them, and who to reach out to with questions or issues arising during these events (Table 4).
And I think that was the first time I remember that our division felt the impact of how close it was and that we didn’t have a disaster plan ready...But it’s hard to say, well, we have a disaster plan. But do we ever practice it? Do I know what’s in it? And I’m going to be honest, I don’t know what’s in it. (Physician, Hospital)
Those who felt more confident about emergency preparedness often developed this knowledge in roles outside their clinical scope. Providers working directly in emergency planning or alongside local public health departments were generally aware of current facility and county plans, such as Hospital Incident Command System (HICS) activation, Mass Casualty Incident (MCI) policies, and All-Hazards approaches, and cited a range of outreach channels, including fliers, media alerts, and disaster preparedness websites, though uptake of these resources was variable.
Nevertheless, despite being aware of and sometimes participating in planning, many providers remained concerned that they were inadequately prepared.
So there’s, I would say, pretty extensive planning, and sort of stockpiling of resources, although it’s difficult to always predict both the severity and the length of these climate related surges when they happen. So we do a lot of planning, but it always still feels like we’re still somewhat unprepared when it actually happens. (Physician, Hospital)
Lack of guidance around best practices. Providers felt that city or county planning and community education can mitigate patient surges. However, local clinics often lacked clarity and guidance around best practices, including thresholds for enacting plans or closing clinics. Clinician leaders felt inadequately prepared or supported when managing operations during these events, often feeling that decisions were being made ad hoc and in isolation (Table 4)
Lack of prioritization and funding for climate emergencies. Providers cited several barriers to planning and mitigation, including insufficient information and funding, unclear responsibility for planning, and limited confidence in their ability to undertake it. Conflicting priorities were also seen as a barrier to addressing climate events; some noted that local departments of public health had focused their efforts on COVID-19 response during the pandemic, so that guidance related to disaster preparedness had not been prioritized. Earthquake preparation was also seen as a higher priority (Table 4).
Limited and deprioritized planning and resource allocation in these larger institutions was sometimes attributed to a perception that climate related events are rare or not locally impactful. The unpredictability of the events was seen as a barrier to an effective and organized response; also mentioned were the difficulty of budgeting for equipment that sits in storage, lack of funding or personnel during events, and lack of funding for preparedness efforts in general (Table 4). The European Commission proposed a 22nd sanctions package against Russia targeting banks, cryptocurrency networks, energy services, the shadow fleet, Russian former combatants, and entities supporting Moscow’s military industry, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced on November 23.
The package focuses on four areas: Russia’s financing, energy sector, participation in European sporting and cultural events, and visa restrictions.
In the financial sector, the Commission proposed expanding restrictions on around 60 Russian banks, including cutting them off from the SWIFT international financial messaging system.
Brussels also plans to strengthen measures against cryptocurrency networks used to finance Russia and circumvent sanctions, with a dedicated cryptocurrency sanctions task force established for that work.
“We will focus on Russia, but we will also add third countries that help it circumvent our sanctions,” von der Leyen stated.
She added that combating sanctions circumvention would be a major element of the package and an area where the EU intends to coordinate with international partners.
The Commission also proposed expanding restrictions on energy-related services to prevent European companies from helping Russia build, operate, or repair energy infrastructure, including oil refineries.
For the first time, the proposed restrictions would also cover services connected to Russia’s electricity sector.
More than 70 additional vessels would be added to the EU sanctions list targeting Russia’s shadow fleet. The Commission also proposed banning tanker vessels insured in Russia.
Another part of the package would prohibit Russian former combatants from entering the European Union.
“We have recently witnessed an escalation of unconventional kinetic operations by Russian operatives in Europe,” von der Leyen stated.
“Former Russian combatants pose a security threat to Europe. They cannot be allowed to move freely across our countries. Therefore, they will be banned from entering the European Union.”
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas also announced proposed measures targeting the Russian and Belarusian military-industrial sectors.
More than 100 additional entries would be added to the sanctions list, including companies involved in circumventing EU restrictions. Export controls would also be tightened against more than 20 entities, while additional goods that could contribute to Russia’s war against Ukraine would face export restrictions.
Restrictions on Russian former combatants had already been under discussion before the package was unveiled. On November 16, Kallas confirmed that the EU was considering a bloc-wide entry ban for Russians who participated in the full-scale invasion, although some member states still had questions about its implementation.

Brussels, 23 November 2026
Today, alongside the proposal for the EU’s 22nd sanctions package, the Commission is taking action to strengthen Europe’s security, ensuring that those linked to Russia’s war of aggression are banned from our territory and cannot become a security risk or the Union and its citizens.
The Commission has today adopted revised guidelines to support the implementation of the visa ban on current and former combatants, as set out in the 21st sanctions package and today’s proposal for the 22nd sanctions package.
The revised guidelines are accompanied by an updated list of supporting documents for Russian visa applicants. They also include stricter measures on tourist visas and on individual artists traveling to the EU as well as guidance on how to implement the proposed ban for Russian athletes from competing on behalf of Russia at sport events in the EU. Together, these measures underline the EU’s determination to apply sustained political pressure on Russia and those connected to its aggression and do not accept a return to business as usual until a just and lasting peace for Ukraine is achieved.
Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission, said: “We have proposed to activate an EU visa ban for anyone who is serving or has served in Russia’s Armed forces since the beginning of its war of aggression. As we see a rise in non-conventional kinetic activities of Russian operatives across Member States, this ban is part of our response. Entry to the European Union must be off limits for those that pose a security risk to Europe”.
Visa ban on ex and current Russian combatants
Following the 21st sanctions package, the Commission and the High Representative have today put forward the necessary initiatives to propose the activation of the EU visa ban for anyone who is serving or has served in the Russian Armed Forces since the beginning of Russia’s war of aggression. With today’s guidelines and supporting documents, Member States will have the tools necessary to put this ban in practice.
- Enhanced checks should focus on individuals who are serving or have served in Russian armed forces or associated armed groups since 24 February 2022 and directly participated in combat operations in Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. Combatants of the Russian Armed Forces of other nationalities are also subject to the visa ban because they represent an equal threat to EU security.
- The updated list of supporting documents provides additional elements for national authorities to identify Russian combatants – such as a questionnaire regarding military service, a self-declaration, and the possibility to request documents, such as a military booklet.
Stricter rules for non-essential travel
- Russian nationals continue to pose high security risks for the European Union, including hybrid threats, disinformation, acts of sabotage and espionage, and other hostile activities. Therefore, the updated guidelines recommend a very strict approach to issuing tourist visas for Russians. Member States should no longer recognise non-biometric Russian passports given high fraud and security risks.
- Stronger checks at EU external borders should be conducted by border guards with thorough individual assessments of all Russian nationals seeking to enter the Schengen area, regardless of where they have travelled from.
- Checks should include interviews and systematic fingerprint checks in the Schengen Information System (SIS). Member States are encouraged to enter SIS alerts following individual decisions to refuse entry on public policy or internal security grounds, to prevent entry from entering through another border crossing.
New measures on Russian athletes and individual artists
Today’s updated guidelines also align with today’s proposal for the 22nd package for a ban on Russian nationals to compete on behalf of the Russian state at sporting events in the EU. When that ban is adopted, Member States notably should consider refusing Schengen visas to Russian athletes competing in sporting events where Russian national symbols such as the flag, anthem, or uniforms are used.
The guidelines call as well for specific attention to be given to individual artists participating in cultural events, who are sponsored by the Russian authorities and who can use their visibility in favour of Russia’s war of aggression.
Next steps
The Commission will work with Member States to support consistent and harmonised implementation of the guidelines and the revised list of supporting documents.
Following the adoption by the Commission of the revised guidelines and the list of supporting documents, the High Representative has put forward the proposal to start applying the visa ban on Russian combatants concerning restrictive measures towards Russia. The Council will then decide when the visa ban on Russian combatants enters into force across the EU.
Background
In 2022, the EU fully suspended the visa facilitation agreement with Russia. Since 2022, the Commission adopted additional measures to stop facilitating visa issuance for Russian nationals. This led to reducing visa issuance. The measures adopted today will further support Member States in their visa application assessment at consulates and at the EU’s external borders in identifying the persons concerned and applying the relevant restrictions. The Commission continues to monitor their implementation and work with Member States to ensure consistent application.
The EU maintains safeguards for those needing protection. Enhanced scrutiny must not prevent entry by people with a legitimate interest in leaving Russia, notably human rights defenders, dissidents and independent journalists. Humanitarian exceptions should also be considered for Ukrainians who were forcibly granted Russian nationality and can prove their previous Ukrainian citizenship.

Good afternoon,
Today, we present our 22nd package of sanctions. The aim is to keep pressure on Russia to end their war of aggression in Ukraine. And we will continue to propose new sanctions until Russia shows genuine intent for a lasting peace in Ukraine. With this package, we are increasing the pressure in three ways. We are striking harder at Russia’s ways to finance its war by targeting its banks and crypto platforms. We are further isolating Russia. We are shutting the door to its participation to European sports and cultural events. We are tightening our visa rules. And we are doubling down on enforcement.
Allow me to go into some of the key elements. First, on financial services. We are extending the transaction ban to some 60 Russian banks. All 60 banks will be removed from the SWIFT system. And we are cracking down on the crypto and payment networks. We will focus on Russia but also include third countries that help Russia to evade our sanctions. This is a major focus of our new package. And an important area where we want to align efforts with international partners. This is the reason why we have also launched a Crypto Sanctions Task Force to support this work.
Second, on the Russian energy sector. We are expanding the energy services ban so that no European company can help Russia build, operate or repair its energy infrastructures, and notably its refineries. For the first time, this ban also covers electricity services. On the Russian Shadow Fleet, we are listing over 70 more ships. And we are proposing to ban all tanker vessels which are insured in Russia.
Third, we have proposed a visa ban for Russian ex-combatants. We have recently seen an escalation in non-conventional kinetic activities of Russian operatives in Europe. And this ban is a part of our response. Russian ex-combatants pose a security risk to Europe. They cannot be allowed to wander freely across our countries. Today, for any sports events in the EU, we are introducing bans on Russian teams and athletes competing under the Russian flag. We propose to ban the display of official Russian symbols. We will also restrict financial flows from Russian sponsors to European-based sports and cultural associations. And we will introduce restrictions on Russians holding posts in governing bodies of European based sports federations.

On 23 November 2026, the EU Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA) issued two public consultations on draft Regulatory Technical Standards (RTSs) for the functioning of anti-money laundering / countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) supervisory colleges in the financial and non-financial sectors.
The draft RTS provide a framework for cooperation, coordination and information exchange between supervisors responsible for the oversight of entities or groups operating in more than one Member State.
Financial sector
The draft RTS establishes conditions for conditions for the functioning of AML/CFT colleges in the financial sector. Accordingly, the draft RTS preserves continuity with supervisory practices that have proven effective by retaining the core elements under the framework set out in the Joint Guidelines on cooperation and information exchange between competent authorities supervising credit and financial institutions under Directive (EU) 2015/849, issued by the European Supervisory Authorities in December 2019.
Non-financial sector
While building on the lessons learned from the operation of AML/CFT supervisory colleges in the financial sector, the draft RTS considers both the different institutional architecture envisaged under Directive (EU) 2024/1640 and the less mature supervisory cooperation arrangements in the non-financial sector. Consequently, the draft RTS comprises provisions addressing issues that are particularly relevant in the non-financial sector. These include the involvement of self-regulatory bodies and the public authorities responsible for their oversight, the handling of information protected by legal privilege, and supervisory arrangements involving a coordinating supervisor where supervisory responsibilities are fragmented across multiple competent authorities and more structured discussions on the need for coordinated supervisory approaches.
Next steps
The deadline for comments on both consultations is 23 December 2026.
Public hearings will take place on 14 December 2026: the financial sector session from 10:00 to 12:00 CET and the non-financial sector session from 14:00 to 16:00 CET.
AMLA first report on supervisory colleagues
AMLA has also published its first report on cooperation of supervisory authorities in AML/CFT colleges, covering the period from 15 November 2025 to 15 July 2026. The report draws on AMLA’s participation in 17 AML/CFT college meetings and identifies good practices observed across colleges, as well as areas where cooperation and information exchange could be further strengthened. The findings in the report have informed AMLA’s ongoing work on the draft RTS on AML/CFT colleges and on its methodology for selecting and participating in colleges.

Listen to this essay
26 minute listen
As I write these words, surface water temperatures across a great swath of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean have been rising for months. El Niño is the name for the recurring and sustained warming of this part of the Pacific. And temperatures are soaring to such highs, relative to their long-term averages, that the El Niño of 2026 may be the strongest in 1,000 years.
It’s still uncertain how the warming ocean will reshape global weather in the months to come, let alone how ecosystems – and human populations – will respond. The future is always murky. Still, when it comes to El Niño, the past could teach us what to expect. And not just the recent past, but also the deep past recently recovered by scientists, historians and archaeologists.
I’m an environmental historian. I work with climatologists to understand how climates have changed in the past. I study how communities understood and adapted to the climate’s changes. And my research suggests that history can help us understand even the most extreme events in today’s rapidly warming climate.
The past can help us see why El Niño is so hard to forecast, for example, or even define. It can show us that, while El Niño has contributed to the deaths of millions of people in the past, it has also enabled others to amass wealth and power.
El Niño indisputably scrambles worldwide weather patterns, but history teaches us that it’s as much a human creation as a natural reality. And this context may help us weather not only the effects of the 2026-27 El Niño in the months to come, but also El Niño’s future on a warming planet.
A vast current of cold water snakes up the western coast of South America. In December each year, that current breaks down for about a month. An influx of warm water delivers tropical fish and – because warm water evaporates more readily than cold water – abundant rainfall.
It’s impossible to know when people first noticed this annual reversal of water temperatures and precipitation. We do know that, sometime after the 16th-century Spanish conquest of the Inka Empire, fishermen named it El Niño, meaning literally ‘the boy’ or, when capitalised, ‘The Christ Child’. At least the reason for the name seems clear: the reversal of current happens around Christmas.
The colonised heartland of the Inka Empire, now known as Peru, won its independence in the 19th century. Towards the end of that century, Peru’s government joined many of its counterparts by establishing a society of geographers to describe the country’s environment and to catalogue its resources. In 1892, the society’s vice president, Camilo Carrillo, introduced the annual switch in water temperatures – and the term El Niño – to the scientific community.
When it entered scientific nomenclature, El Niño was therefore a cycle that was small in time (involving just one month every year), space (affecting only the Peruvian coast), and perceived importance (interesting only to a handful of local scientists).
El Niño is actually the oceanic expression of a colossal seesaw of atmospheric pressure over the Pacific
Only gradually did researchers detect a much bigger oscillation in Pacific Ocean temperatures, one that happened every two to seven years. This oscillation was eventually branded as El Niño. By the end of the 20th century, the effort to forecast its onset and worldwide impacts became a quintessential example of big, state-supported science.
The modern version of El Niño seems easy to define. It’s a dramatic warming of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean – a warming that’s confined to the tropics, lasts for many months, and tends to peak around the end of the year. It transfers a stupendous quantity of heat and moisture into the atmosphere, which the tropical jet stream redistributes, reshuffling weather patterns from one region to another.
But what causes these recurring warmings of Pacific Ocean water? And how, exactly, do they affect regional weather patterns?
Only recently have scientists been able to answer those questions. It turns out that El Niño is actually the oceanic expression of a colossal seesaw of atmospheric pressure over the Pacific Ocean, known as the Southern Oscillation. When air is tightly packed together over the eastern Pacific – when atmospheric pressure there is high, in other words – and when it’s low over the western Pacific, the pressure difference reinforces persistent winds that blow west along the equator.
These trade winds, as they’re called, can push so much warm surface water into the tropics of the western Pacific that they allow deeper, colder water to reach the top of the eastern Pacific. This is called La Niña. But when the difference in Pacific Ocean pressure dips, the trade winds falter, and the warm water of the western Pacific surges east. This we call El Niño.
Scientists have learned that the Southern Oscillation involves reinforcing relationships, known as feedbacks, between the air and sea. Usually, hot water in the western Pacific evaporates in towering storms, releasing heat. The air flows east, cools down, grows denser, falls, then surges back to the west, warming up.
This pattern, known as the Walker Circulation, strengthens the pressure differences of the Southern Oscillation and fuels the trade winds. But during an El Niño, warm water, evaporation and rains shift to the eastern Pacific, weakening transpacific differences in pressure and, in turn, the trade winds. This pattern helps explain the most important weather associated with El Niño: torrential rains across parts of the Western Hemisphere, and drought in Australasia.
Today, El Niño seems less like an event, and more like one end of a seesaw that perpetually teeters across the Pacific. But why does the seesaw behave as it does? There is still no scientific consensus, but the historical traces of both human societies and the natural world provide us with clues.
The most important questions about El Niño concern its impacts on global weather patterns – or in other words, the teleconnections that form between the warming of the equatorial Pacific and droughts, floods, storms or heatwaves around the world.
These teleconnections are usually presented as predictable and consistent from one El Niño to the next. They’re visualised in maps that supposedly depict how regional temperatures or precipitation change as El Niño intensifies in the Pacific Ocean
But no two El Niño events have exactly the same teleconnections. One reason is that the extent, intensity and duration of unusually warm water in the tropical Pacific differs from one El Niño to the next. Another is that El Niño is only one of many influences on regional weather, and its effects generally weaken with distance from the tropical Pacific.
Because El Niño’s impacts on regional weather are never identical, it’s impossible to predict exactly how a future El Niño will impact most of the world’s people and ecosystems. But it’s even harder to piece together the history of El Niño before the beginning of the 20th century, when ships began to regularly measure sea-surface temperatures. And it’s harder still before the middle of the 19th century, when scientists began to systematically gather data from rain gauges where El Niño reliably generates heavy precipitation.
Decades of research now reveals broad patterns in El Niño history that could give a rough sense of what’s in store
It’s a challenge, but not impossible. Climatologists – and a handful of historians and geographers – estimate the timing, strength and impacts of El Niño before the mid-19th century by consulting what they call the ‘archives of society’ and the ‘archives of nature’.
The archives of society were created by the people of the past. They include surviving texts that describe weather directly, such as the logbooks that sailors wrote aboard ships. They also include diverse sources of evidence – not only documents but also artefacts, ruins, even oral traditions – that record human activities so dependent on the weather that they can serve as proxies for it.
Unlike the archives of society, the archives of nature were created by Earth itself (even if they are, of course, interpreted by people). These archives are parts of the natural world that responded either to changes in the water temperature of the Pacific Ocean, or to the regional extremes in temperature and precipitation that can be associated with those changes. The responses leave a mark in natural archives, changing the composition of growth rings in trees or corals, for example. Each mark serves as a proxy for El Niño conditions in the distant past.
Neither societal nor natural archives can provide direct measurements of sea-surface temperatures or weather, so histories of El Niño are inevitably full of uncertainty. Trees, for example, can only grow (or stop growing) so much. It’s one reason why their rings can’t precisely measure the strength of past El Niño events (and one reason why we can’t easily pin down whether this year’s El Niño really is the strongest in a millennium).
Still, decades of research can now reveal three broad patterns in El Niño history that could give us a rough sense of what’s in store – not only in the coming year, but in our future on a warming world.
Above all, El Niño shaped humanity’s past by suddenly changing where water was available, how much there was, and how people could use it.
The foundations of human life – food, shelter and movement – depend to varying degrees on water. Human populations can use water in many different ways, so they have learned to thrive in very different environments. But it seems to have been much harder for them to adapt to the sudden disruptions in water that a strong El Niño – or that a trend towards stronger El Niño conditions overall – could bring about.
This is the first pattern in El Niño’s human history.
We can already see its outlines a little more than 4,000 years ago, when the first states and empires established themselves. At that time, El Niño conditions seem to have grown more frequent, intense and long-lasting. The reason may have been a multimillennial cycle in the wobble of Earth’s rotation that altered the amount of sunlight associated with different seasons, weakening the trade winds.
It all sounds convincing until – inevitably – new evidence emerges
Natural and societal archives suggest that some communities withered as El Niño intensified. In Peru, for example, populations appear to have deserted temple mounds, giant platforms that supported elaborate buildings and plazas. It’s easy to imagine that torrential floods sparked by strong El Niño conditions made it impossible to maintain these structures. But archaeological evidence hints at other changes that might have been partly responsible for population movements, including new trade networks and newly cultivated plants. How much can the coincidence of two trends really tell us about causation?
Maybe quite a lot, if similar coincidences pop up elsewhere. And it seems they do. A little under 3,000 years ago, for example, settlers established a community at Teouma, on the island of Efate in today’s Vanuatu. Chemical traces of human waste and leaves in nearby swamp sediments show that the settlers cultivated taro, a root vegetable, during a period of increasing rainfall. By around 2,600 years ago, however, a trend towards stronger or more frequent El Niño conditions seems to have made local rainfall more erratic. The trend appears to correlate with a decline in settlement and cultivation on Efate.
You’ll notice a lot of conditional language about possible changes and potential correlations. Deep history is like that. Natural and societal archives can let us identify probable trends, figure out roughly when they happened, and craft convincing theories for how one trend caused another. It all sounds convincing until – inevitably – new evidence emerges that compels us to re-date a trend, or propose another cause for it.
In general, evidence from the archives of nature and society is more abundant and precise the closer it dates to our present. Evidence from the previous millennium lets us identify not just trends in human and El Niño history, but discrete events.
Catastrophic famines partly linked to strong El Niño conditions appear to have killed millions
By the 16th century, for example, cave formations, tree rings and reports written by government officials let us reconstruct the likely impacts of individual El Niño years on the Indian summer monsoon. They reveal a series of devastating droughts across India in the late 16th century, the middle and end of the 17th century, and the late 18th century.
It may be that a series of explosive volcanic eruptions were partly responsible for these droughts. The cooling effect of the sulphur they launched into the upper atmosphere altered temperature differences between latitudes, and between land and water. These differences in temperature help create the winds that bring monsoon rains; when they changed, the rains did too.
But the droughts also coincided with El Niño conditions. In fact, there may be a connection, because the new wind patterns created by powerful eruptions seem to warm the eastern Pacific, relative to the west. Regardless, El Niño can also weaken the Indian monsoon by shifting warm water and rising air eastward across the tropical Pacific.
When the monsoon rains failed, harvests could too. Of course, rural populations and states had many ways of protecting themselves. Wells and granaries stored water and seeds, for instance, while trade networks could allow for emergency food imports. Still, these systems broke down when droughts lasted too long – and especially when states waged war.
In some El Niño events and in some parts of India, droughts provoked widespread famine only when armies demanded food from the already depleted countryside. In other Indian regions, the death toll soared when widespread malnutrition joined migration from drought-stricken regions to encourage the spread of epidemic disease. All told, catastrophic famines partly linked to strong El Niño conditions appear to have killed millions across 16th-, 17th- and 18th-century India.
Everywhere El Niño sparked extreme weather, communities suffered. Yet some prospered at their expense, and this is the second pattern we can discern in El Niño’s history.
The collapse of China’s Ming dynasty in the 17th century seems to provide a striking example. Growth rings in trees and corals indicate that El Niño conditions repeatedly contributed to a weakening of the East Asian monsoon in the late 16th and early 17th centuries. At first, droughts afflicted both northeastern China – home of the loosely connected Jurchen peoples – and northern China, the Ming heartland.
In the diverse environments of northeastern China, the Jurchen hunted, fished and farmed, a varied subsistence strategy that gave them some protection from drought. They also raided across the Great Wall into Ming territory, where they seized stockpiled grain. Eventually, droughts intensified in northern China, where soaring food prices and famine helped to destabilise the Ming regime. But drought seems to have yielded to above-average rainfall in Jurchen territories. Food provided by plentiful rain may have aided efforts to consolidate Jurchen communities into a united ‘Manchu’ state that was strong enough to exploit the Ming dynasty’s weakness, conquer China, and establish a new Qing dynasty.
Indeed, conquest and colonialism created a means by which the impacts of El Niño could be amplified for some communities, but alleviated or even exploited for others. This redistribution of vulnerability was never clearer or more catastrophic than in the late 19th century, when exceptionally strong El Niño conditions coincided with a global age of imperialism.
The exact connection between colonialism and crisis differed from place to place
In 1876, drought spread across India, then intensified with a strong El Niño in 1877-78. It was the heyday of the British Raj. Colonial officials had upended lives and livelihoods in many Indian farming communities by forcing them to plant cash crops such as tea or cotton. Now, there wasn’t enough food to go round. What grain could be harvested was either redirected from the poorest communities to areas where people could pay more, or exported out of India by colonial administrators who scorned market interventions.
Tens of millions died in the ensuing famines.
Similar tragedies played out wherever El Niño sparked drought in the late 19th century, though the exact connection between colonialism and crisis differed from place to place. In Eritrea and Ethiopia, for instance, Italian invaders arrived with cattle infected by rinderpest, a deadly disease that spread to local cattle before the arrival of another strong El Niño in 1890-91. Widespread mortality among cattle intensified food shortages, as did the arrival of immense locust swarms.
Perhaps a third of Ethiopia’s population perished.
The United States, however, often benefitted from El Niño conditions. As worldwide droughts drove up grain prices in 1877-78, US farmers exported enormous quantities of wheat to Europe. The resulting inflow of gold-backed credit strengthened US finances, and helped the government manage its Civil War debts. A century later, during another strong El Niño in 1972, the collapse of the Peruvian anchovy fishery, owing both to warming water and years of overfishing, deprived poultry producers of fishmeal. But that allowed US farmers to profit by planting soy, a substitute. In the even stronger 1982-83 event, torrential rains devastated California and other southern states, but overall, the US economy received a powerful stimulus from mild winter weather.
It was around this time – the late 20th century – that scientists and journalists created the modern concept of El Niño as a global event that recurred every few years to cause predictable disasters. This is the third pattern in our history. El Niño is not just an environmental reality; it’s also a cultural reality: a manufactured threat that is a unique product of our time.
In some respects, that threat was a creation of the 1957-58 International Geophysical Year (IGY). During the IGY, a global campaign to observe Earth and near-Earth space served as an arena for scientific and technological competition between the US and Soviet governments. The IGY fortuitously coincided with an El Niño, and unprecedented observations helped scientists begin to understand the true dimensions of Pacific Ocean warming.
It turned out that different El Niño events strengthened in different ways
Cold War politics continued to shape El Niño science. The 1959 Cuban Revolution joined the growing importance – for poultry farmers – of the Peruvian anchovy fishery to spur US support for collaborations between US and Latin American scientists. These collaborations, many of which focused on the study of El Niño, were supposed to demonstrate the value of partnership with US institutions.
When navies deployed nuclear submarines to reinforce newly developed nuclear arsenals, they began to fund oceanographic research partly to better understand the underwater battlespace. Until then, oceanographers had been able to visit marine environments only occasionally, in ships. Beginning in the 1950s, new funds and technology allowed them to deploy instruments to monitor environments continuously, for months or years at a time.
The launch of Sputnik 1 during the IGY also heralded a new age in which weather satellites kept the oceans under constant supervision from above. And computer models soon seemed capable of forecasting not just global warming, but also the state of the Southern Oscillation. By the early 1980s, prominent scientists believed that El Niño could finally be predicted months in advance.
Yet the strong El Niño of 1982-83 came as a shock to the overwhelming majority of meteorologists and oceanographers. It turned out that different El Niño events strengthened in different ways, and each had distinct impacts on regional weather patterns. Because the unanticipated El Niño led to floods, droughts and storms that killed thousands of people, inflicted billions of dollars in damage, and cost the global economy trillions in estimated lost growth, scientists redoubled their efforts to forecast El Niño and its teleconnections.
The concept of El Niño as a global disaster had deep roots in the history of US mass media
In 1985, the World Meteorological Organization – a United Nations agency – launched a decade-long project to scatter ocean-monitoring buoys across the tropical Pacific. Scientists also began to use both societal and natural archives to reconstruct the deep history of El Niño. In early 1997, they had learned enough to successfully predict another ocean warming months before it happened. Scientists from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) alerted US journalists, and they created a media sensation: an El Niño reimagined as a looming, worldwide catastrophe.
It’s ironic that American journalists developed this threatening new view of El Niño. In the US, the economic benefits of the 1997-98 El Niño would again far outweigh the damage. But the concept of El Niño as a global disaster had deep roots in the history of US mass media.
Since the 19th century, US reporters had thrilled audiences by portraying natural phenomena as sensational, often threatening events – events that could be understood only by plucky scientists. A close but routine approach of a comet or planet to Earth, for example, became a brush with death recorded by swashbuckling scientists in far-flung observatories.
It was journalism that resonated in a culture shaped by religious concepts of a purifying apocalypse. And it helps explain why, in the 20th century, the scientific investigation of changes in the atmosphere – not just global warming, but also nuclear winter, the ozone hole, acid rain, and even the potential consequences of asteroid impacts or volcanic eruptions – relied on US funding and institutions, while coming to particularly alarm US citizens.
Now, some US journalists used the Spanish name of El Niño to conjure an image of a foreign menace that several compared to migrants from South America. As the 1997-98 El Niño warmed into the strongest event since the 19th century, ‘Blame it on El Niño’ and ‘Don’t blame me, blame El Niño!’ were common slogans on everything from bumper stickers to T-shirts. That was true even though scientists couldn’t predict exactly how El Niño would affect weather in most parts of the world, let alone how populations would react.
It was in 1997 that today’s understanding of El Niño – part Cold War relic, part scientific achievement, and part media monster – was born.
The patterns in El Niño’s past teach us that the warming of the tropical Pacific can be disastrous for communities exposed to droughts and floods. But they also reveal that El Niño disasters are caused less by the severity of weather extremes, and more by the brutality of how some communities are exploited by others. They suggest that today’s imagined El Niño – a global threat, with predictable impacts on weather – is less an accurate reflection of reality than a creation of modern science, media and geopolitics.
In the coming years and decades, it’s likely that El Niño’s impacts on populations will be shaped primarily by human relationships and ideas, not by nature. But human actions now include greenhouse gas pollution on such a scale that Earth has warmed by about 1.5°C, relative to its average temperature in the late 19th century. This pollution is supercharging the impacts of El Niño on weather. Heatwaves are growing hotter, and intensifying evaporation means droughts are getting worse. Partly because a warm atmosphere holds more water, downpours are ever more intense.
Global warming doesn’t seem capable of ending the Southern Oscillation, and with it the age-old seesaw of El Niño and La Niña. Still, it could lead to even more intense El Niño events that cause even more extreme weather.
It’s never been more urgent to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. But El Niño’s past also teaches us a deeper lesson about adapting to climatic extremes. Today, the world seems increasingly shaped by renewed great power competition: by militarism and colonial relationships between superpowers and their patrons. History suggests that such a world could be one in which millions die unnecessarily, not just through war but in preventable climate disasters.
It’s a warning from the past that today’s governments would be wise to heed, as El Niño reshapes environments from one end of the world to another in the months and years to come.
